# Rust secure coding

- Keep untrusted data in validated domain types and propagate recoverable errors with `Result`. Do not `unwrap`, `expect`, or index directly on attacker-controlled input in server paths.
- Use parameterized database APIs (`sqlx`, Diesel, driver binds). Never construct query text with `format!` using untrusted values.
- Use `std::process::Command` with a fixed program and `.arg` elements. Do not invoke a shell with untrusted data.
- Use `OsRng` or an approved CSPRNG for security values. Avoid deterministic/non-cryptographic RNGs for keys, tokens, nonces, and reset links.
- Minimize and isolate `unsafe`, FFI, `transmute`, raw pointers, and manual `Send`/`Sync`. Document the exact validity, aliasing, bounds, lifetime, alignment, and concurrency invariants.
- Validate pointers, lengths, ownership, encodings, NUL termination, and return codes at every FFI boundary. Do not let a foreign panic/unwind cross an unsupported ABI boundary.
- Hold synchronization across the complete state invariant. Avoid check-then-act races, lock-order cycles, unbounded channels/tasks, and blocking work on async executors.
- Bound allocation, input/body size, recursion, decompression, regex, task concurrency, and external-call time. Avoid cloning attacker-sized data unnecessarily.
- Canonicalize and verify path confinement with symlink/race considerations. Use safe temporary-file APIs and restrictive permissions.
- Prefer data-only serialization and explicit enums. Do not dynamically load untrusted native libraries/plugins or treat deserialization validation as authorization.
- Avoid leaking secrets through `Debug`, panic messages, traces, or error chains returned to clients. Use secrecy/zeroization types where the threat model requires them.
- Keep `cargo audit`, lockfiles, clippy/static checks, overflow checks where appropriate, and unsafe-code policy intact.
